opus-5.5.text:
I think "black box" is a phrase people use a bit loosely, so it's worth separating a few meanings.

At one level, a language model is the opposite of a black box. We know exactly what it is: we wrote the architecture, we know every operation, every weight is sitting there in memory and you can read it out. Nothing is hidden in the literal sense. If you want to know what the model computes on a given input, you can trace every multiplication.

The problem is that knowing every step doesn't mean you understand what's happening. It's a bit like the brain: knowing every neuron's firing doesn't tell you why someone made a decision. We have billions of parameters, and the behavior we care about, like reasoning, planning, or deciding to refuse something, isn't stored in any one place. It's distributed and emerges from the interaction of many components. So "black box" really means we lack a good *level of description*. We can describe it at the lowest level and at the highest behavioral level, but the middle layer, the concepts and algorithms it actually uses, is still mostly missing.

There's another sense that I think is more important: even the people training these models often can't predict what capabilities will come out. You change the data mix or scale up, and some ability appears or disappears, and we explain it afterward rather than predicting it. Training is closer to cultivating than engineering. In that sense it's a black box not because the internals are hidden, but because our theory hasn't caught up with our practice.

That said, I don't think we should be too pessimistic. Interpretability research has made real progress: finding features that correspond to concepts, tracing circuits for specific behaviors, even steering models by intervening on internal representations. And from a behavioral point of view we can do a lot of science, careful experiments, controlled evaluations, much as psychology studies humans without fully understanding neurons.

So my view is that it's not a fundamentally unknowable black box. It's a very complex system we built faster than we learned to understand it. The gap is real and it matters for safety and reliability, but it's a research problem, not a mystery.

r002.rationale: It says black-box status depends on the level of description: operations are known at the lowest level, behavior is visible at the highest, while the middle layer remains poorly understood.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the "black box" claim is half right, and the half that's wrong matters a lot.

It's right in a narrow mechanistic sense. If you ask me why a particular model produced a particular token, I can't point to a line of code the way I could for a compiler or a database. There are hundreds of billions of parameters, and we don't have a clean story that maps individual weights to behaviors. Interpretability research is making progress, but we're still very far from reading a model the way you'd read a program.

But people hear "black box" and jump to "we have no idea how it works," and that's just not true. There are several layers where we actually understand quite a lot.

The first is the training process. We know exactly what the objective is. Next-token prediction on internet-scale text, and then reinforcement learning on top of that. The objective shapes everything. When I was working on ReAct and later on agents, almost every surprising behavior we saw could be traced back to what the pretraining data rewarded. If a model is good at writing Python but bad at some obscure language, that's not mysterious. The data told you that already.

The second layer is behavior. You can treat the model as an empirical object, like a biologist treats an organism. You design experiments, you perturb the inputs, you look at how the outputs change. A lot of my own work has been this kind of thing. Tree of Thoughts, for example, came out of asking a very concrete question: when the model fails a reasoning task, does it fail because it can't generate the right step, or because it can't evaluate and backtrack? That's a question you can actually answer with experiments, even without opening the weights. And it turned out to be the second one, which told us what to build.

The third layer is the environment and the feedback loop. Especially with agents, I'd argue the model is becoming the less mysterious part. The thing that's hard to reason about is the system: the model plus the tools plus the environment plus the reward signal. If you give a model a coding environment and a test suite, the behavior you get is determined as much by what the tests reward as by whatever is going on inside the network. So "black box" sort of locates the difficulty in the wrong place. I'd rather people think about where the data and rewards come from, because that's where you actually have control.

There's one more thing I'd say. Humans are black boxes too. I can't explain exactly why I chose a particular word just now. We've never required mechanistic transparency as a precondition for trusting a doctor or a pilot. We trust them because of training, track record, and evaluation. I think the honest position on language models is similar. We should push hard on interpretability, but in the meantime the real work is building good evaluations and good environments, because that's what actually makes the systems reliable.

So, a black box in the mechanistic sense, yes. But a very well-studied, very steerable black box, where most of the levers are in the data and the environment rather than inside the weights.

r002.rationale: It makes the black-box claim depend on the level considered: models are black boxes in a narrow mechanistic sense, while training, behavior, and feedback loops are substantially understood.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish two meanings of “black box.” One is that we don’t know how the system is built. That’s not really true of language models: we know the architecture, the training objective, and how the parameters are updated. The other is that, even knowing those things, we can’t fully explain why a particular input produces a particular output. In that sense, they are black boxes.

The interesting gap is between understanding the mechanism and understanding the behavior. You can describe every computation in a model without having a useful explanation of why it solved one problem and failed on another. Looking at billions of parameter values doesn’t automatically give you that explanation.

But I wouldn’t treat this as an all-or-nothing property. We can run controlled experiments, change the input, inspect internal activations, and intervene on parts of the model. Those approaches give us different kinds of understanding, even if none gives us a complete picture. And asking the model to explain itself isn’t enough—the explanation it generates is also an output we need to examine.

So for me, the useful question is: what exactly do we want to understand, and what evidence would establish that understanding? Explaining an individual answer, predicting when the model will fail, and making its behavior more reliable are related goals, but they aren’t the same goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we first need to ask what we mean by “black box.” There are at least two different questions. One is whether we understand how a language model is built. At that level, a lot is quite clear: we know the architecture, the training objective, and how the parameters are updated. The other is whether we can explain why a trained model gives a particular answer. That is much harder. Knowing the training procedure doesn’t mean we can trace a specific behavior back to a clean, human-readable rule.

But a black box doesn’t mean something we can’t study. We can change the input, intervene in the model, and test hypotheses about its behavior. We can gradually develop an understanding even if we don’t have a complete explanation of every internal computation.

So I would treat “black box” as a description of the limits of our current understanding, rather than a conclusion that understanding is impossible. And the level of understanding we need depends on the application. If the model is helping you brainstorm, you can judge the output fairly directly. If it’s making a consequential decision, then we need much stronger evidence about when it works, when it fails, and how to keep those failures under control.
